```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The record of the housing-audit case as the Dataverse API lists it, written by
# _model-outputs/build_dataverse_files.R, and the archived copy of its data file
dv_files <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/dataverse_1HOVTU_files.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dv_data <- datawizard::data_filter(dv_files, label == "HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.tab")
md5_archived <- unname(tools::md5sum("../data-raw/housing/dataverse_1HOVTU/HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.dta"))
audit_original <- readr::read_csv("../cases/housing/data/audit_original.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Figures for the section on the published series, read from the series file
# and from the comparison of every option of the full menu with its twins on
# the curve of the claim
series <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/macro/predictor_measures.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(dplyr::between(year, 2004, 2013), !is.na(value))
curve <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
devs <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive", axis == "measure")
tips <- datawizard::data_filter(devs, option == "es_1574_tips")
es_growth <- datawizard::data_filter(devs, option == "es_growth")
coverage <- series |>
  dplyr::summarise(cells = dplyr::n(), countries = dplyr::n_distinct(cntry), .by = measure)
unemp_curve <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, predictor == "unemp")

# Shares printed to one decimal, rounding halves up
measure_share <- sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(forks$share[forks$axis == "measure"] * 10 + 0.5) / 10)
tips_below <- sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(tips$below_zero_sig * 10 + 0.5) / 10)
tips_changes <- sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(tips$class_changes * 10 + 0.5) / 10)
curve_below <- sprintf("%.1f%%", floor(100 * mean(unemp_curve$supports & unemp_curve$sig) * 10 + 0.5) / 10)

# The four full-coverage unemployment series, with the means of each country and
# of each year removed (sequential demeaning is exact on a balanced panel)
full <- c("wb_nat", "es_1574_act", "es_2064_pop", "es_2564_lfs")
within_cor <- series |>
  datawizard::data_filter(measure %in% full) |>
  dplyr::mutate(value = value - mean(value), .by = c(measure, cntry)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(value = value - mean(value), .by = c(measure, year)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = c(cntry, year), names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(full)) |>
  cor()
cor_range <- sprintf("%.3f", range(within_cor[upper.tri(within_cor)]))
names_cy <- readr::read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::distinct(cntry, country)
tips_pre <- series |>
  datawizard::data_filter(measure == "es_1574_tips", year < 2009) |>
  dplyr::distinct(cntry) |>
  dplyr::left_join(names_cy, by = "cntry") |>
  dplyr::pull(country) |>
  sort()
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about where the data that social scientists analyse are held, and how a researcher gets hold of them. The four cases of the course reach a researcher by four different routes. The housing-audit file is one public download from the Harvard Dataverse. The cohabitation unions are built from public-use files that the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) of the United States serves to anyone. The immigration-and-trust data come from the European Social Survey (ESS) under a free registration and an open licence, and the Eurobarometer waves of the EU-frames case come from the GESIS archive under an account and terms of use that forbid passing them on. The files of SCORE and Multi100, the two projects that checked the four claims, sit beside all four on the Open Science Framework (OSF). Section 1 sets out the three kinds of route by which data are reached, section 2 maps the sources that hold most of the quantitative data of sociology, political science and demography, section 3 follows each case from its source to a file on your disk, programmatically where the source allows it and by hand where it does not, and section 4 is about citing what you downloaded.

The routes are taught where the course needs them. In the three-day courses on the [immigration-and-trust](../tracks/trust-three-days/index.qmd), [cohabitation](../tracks/cohabitation-three-days/index.qmd) and [EU-frames](../tracks/eu-frames-three-days/index.qmd) cases, the second session of day 1 reads this module, and the fourth session downloads the raw files of the case by the route that section 3 describes, so that day 2 can build the analysis file from them as the [data management module](data-management.qmd) shows. The self-study track reads the access routes and the map in [stage 5](../tracks/self-study/stage-5.qmd), and downloads the Eurobarometer waves by the GESIS route in [stage 10](../tracks/self-study/stage-10.qmd). The one-day courses download nothing, because the workspace and the browser lab of each case hold its data, and there section 3 explains where those files came from. The [repositories module](repositories.qmd) covers the other side of the exchange, where a finished piece of work is deposited so that others can find it.

Two things are outside the scope of this page. Qualitative data archives are not discussed, although the UK Data Service, which appears in the tables below, and the Qualitative Data Repository both hold qualitative collections. And nothing here replaces the terms of use of a particular dataset, which change, and which you read before you download.

## 1. Three ways in {#sec-access}

Almost every dataset on this page is reached by one of three routes, and the vocabulary of the archives follows them.

**Open download.** The file is on a public page or behind a public API (an interface through which a program, rather than a person at a browser, asks a server for data), under a licence that permits reuse with attribution, typically Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY), a dedication to the public domain such as CC0, or an open government licence. World Bank indicators, the aggregate tables published by Eurostat, the public-use files of the US statistical agencies and most replication packages in political science are of this kind. Nothing is asked of you except the citation and, for official surveys, respect for the rules that protect the respondents.

**Registration and licence.** You create an account under your own name, agree to conditions (no redistribution, no attempt to identify anyone, citation of the source, sometimes non-commercial use), and download. This is the standard route for survey microdata, meaning files with one row per respondent: the European Social Survey, the Eurobarometer at GESIS, the safeguarded collection of the UK Data Service, SHARE, IPUMS. The registration is free, immediate or nearly so, and the archive keeps a record of who took what.

**Application and secure access.** The data are too detailed to leave the archive: linked administrative records, fine geography, exact dates of birth, business microdata. You apply with a project description, your institution may have to be recognised as a research entity, you may have to complete a training course and become an accredited researcher, and you then work either on a scientific-use file sent under contract or inside a secure environment where nothing leaves without being checked. Examples are the microdata held by Eurostat, the controlled collection of the UK Data Service through SecureLab, the Secure Research Service of the Office for National Statistics and the contract route of the German Socio-Economic Panel. Allow weeks or months.

Two distinctions run across all three. **Microdata against aggregates:** a respondent-level file needs the second or third route, while the country-year or region-year tables computed from it are usually open. The EU-frames panel of the course is of that kind, an open aggregate built from licensed microdata. And **catalogue against archive:** a catalogue such as the CESSDA Data Catalogue or re3data tells you that a dataset exists and where it is held, and the archive that holds it is where you register and download.

The four cases cover the first two routes, and they differ in what a course may pass on to its participants.

| Case | Data | Held by | Route | Terms | What the course ships |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Housing audit | The 1,014 emails of the field experiment | Harvard Dataverse, [doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU) | Open download, by hand or through the API of the Dataverse | CC0, a dedication to the public domain | The file itself, as CSV |
| Cohabitation | The female respondent files of the National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG), 1995 and 2006–2010 | NCHS | Open download, no account | Public domain, used under the data use restrictions of NCHS | The unions and person-months built from the files, and the person-month file of SCORE |
| Immigration and trust | ESS rounds 1–4 | ESS ERIC, through the ESS Data Portal run by Sikt | Registration, then download by hand or through the API of the portal | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | An extract of 120,080 respondents, adapted from the ESS under the same licence |
| EU frames | Sixteen waves of the Standard Eurobarometer | GESIS | Registration, download by hand | The terms of use of GESIS, which forbid passing the files on | Country-year aggregates only, under CC BY 4.0 |

: The data of the four cases, the route to each and what the terms allow the course to pass on.

## 2. The map {#sec-map}

The tables name the source, what it holds, how it is reached and where to start. 'Open' means the first route above, 'registration' the second and 'application' the third; the note says what the registration or application involves where that is not obvious. They are a starting point for a question of your own rather than a census of the field.

### 2.1 Cross-national survey programmes {#sec-surveys}

| Source | What it holds | Access | Where to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **European Social Survey (ESS)** | Attitudes, values and behaviour across Europe every two years since 2002; eleven rounds at the time of writing, plus the CRONOS online panels; the source of the immigration-and-trust case | Registration, free; the survey describes its data as "freely accessible data for academics, policymakers, civil society and the wider public" | [ESS Data Portal](https://ess.sikt.no/en/), which searches, builds a custom file and downloads; [section 3.3](#sec-ess) |
| **Eurobarometer** | Surveys run twice a year for the European Commission since 1974, with the Standard, Special and Flash series; the source of the EU-frames case | Registration with GESIS, free for academic use, one study per wave | [GESIS Eurobarometer Data Service](https://www.gesis.org/en/eurobarometer-data-service) and [search.gesis.org](https://search.gesis.org/); [section 3.4](#sec-gesis) |
| **European Values Study (EVS) and World Values Survey (WVS)** | Values and beliefs in waves since 1981; the two are harmonised into a joint file for the 2017 wave | Registration, free; EVS is distributed by GESIS, WVS from its own site | [europeanvaluesstudy.eu](https://europeanvaluesstudy.eu/), [worldvaluessurvey.org](https://www.worldvaluessurvey.org/) |
| **International Social Survey Programme (ISSP)** | One themed module a year since 1985, repeated on a cycle (role of government, social inequality, religion, work) across some forty countries | Registration with GESIS, free | [issp.org](https://issp.org/), files via search.gesis.org |
| **SHARE** | The Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe: a longitudinal panel of people over fifty, with linked administrative records for several countries | Registration, "free of charge for scientific use globally", under published conditions of use | [share-eric.eu](https://share-eric.eu/) |
| **Generations and Gender Programme (GGP)** | Longitudinal surveys on family, fertility and partnership | Registration | [ggp-i.org](https://www.ggp-i.org/) |
| **Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES)** | Post-election surveys harmonised across countries, with system-level variables | Open | [cses.org](https://www.cses.org/) |
| **OECD PISA and PIAAC** | Student assessment (PISA) and adult skills (PIAAC) microdata, with contextual questionnaires | Open download of the public-use files | [PISA databases](https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/pisa-2022-database.html), [PIAAC](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/programmes/piaac.html) |
| **The regional barometers** | Afrobarometer, Latinobarómetro and the Arab Barometer: repeated public-opinion surveys on their continents | Registration or open, by barometer | [afrobarometer.org](https://www.afrobarometer.org/), [latinobarometro.org](https://www.latinobarometro.org/), [arabbarometer.org](https://www.arabbarometer.org/) |

### 2.2 Archives and catalogues {#sec-archives}

| Source | What it holds | Access | Where to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UK Data Service (UKDS)** | The national collection for the UK: the large government surveys, the household panels and cohorts, the census aggregates, ESRC-funded project data, and the international series it distributes. Its three tiers are named "Open" (download without registration), "Safeguarded" (registration and the End User Licence, sometimes a Special Licence with a use statement) and "Controlled" (SecureLab, for accredited researchers whose organisation signs an agreement) | By tier; registration is open to UK academic users through their institution and to others through a separate route | [ukdataservice.ac.uk](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/), [types of data access](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/help/access-policy/types-of-data-access/) |
| **GESIS Data Archive** | Germany's central social-science archive and the distributor of the Eurobarometer, EVS, ISSP, ALLBUS and the European Election Studies; each study is assigned an access category from free download to depositor permission, and the archive runs a Secure Data Center for the sensitive files | Registration, free; category by study | [search.gesis.org](https://search.gesis.org/) |
| **CESSDA Data Catalogue** | The joint catalogue of the European social-science archives (the UK Data Service, GESIS, DANS, Sikt, the Finnish Social Science Data Archive and their peers), searchable in one place; downloads happen at the archive that holds the study | Catalogue open; access by archive | [datacatalogue.cessda.eu](https://datacatalogue.cessda.eu/) |
| **ICPSR** | The Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research at Michigan, the largest social-science archive in the United States; a part of the collection is public, most of it is for members, and restricted files are applied for | Institutional membership for most files; check whether your university is a member | [icpsr.umich.edu](https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/) |
| **Harvard Dataverse** | An open repository run on the Dataverse software, holding tens of thousands of datasets deposited by researchers and journals, including much replication material from political science and the package of the housing-audit case | Open, with terms set per dataset; a public API, and the `dataverse` R package | [dataverse.harvard.edu](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/); [section 3.1](#sec-dataverse) |
| **re3data** | The registry of research data repositories, for finding out which repository holds a kind of data at all | Open | [re3data.org](https://www.re3data.org/) |

## Try it

Pick a question you have worked on, or would like to. Find a dataset that could answer it in two of the catalogues above, the CESSDA Data Catalogue and re3data, and write down for each: the archive that holds it, the access route, and the first step you would have to take on Monday morning. If the two catalogues disagree about where the data are, note the disagreement as well.
:::

## 3. The routes of the four cases {#sec-course}

The subsections run from the most open source to the most restricted: the Dataverse (housing audit), the public-use files of NCHS (cohabitation), the ESS Data Portal (immigration and trust) and the GESIS archive (EU frames), followed by the World Bank, from which two cases take their country-level series, and the OSF, which holds the files of SCORE and Multi100 for all four. Each route is written as steps that you can follow from a fresh R session. Code that downloads is shown and not run on this page, which is built without a connection, and the results printed beside it come from the copies that the course keeps. None of it has to be done for a one-day course, where the data are already in place.

Every download in this section ends with a check that the file is the one that the course used. The simplest check is a checksum: the MD5 sum is a short code computed from the contents of a file, which changes if a single byte of the file changes, so two files with the same MD5 sum are the same file. `tools::md5sum()` computes it in R, and several of the sources publish it beside the file.

### 3.1 The Harvard Dataverse: the housing-audit file {#sec-dataverse}

The original authors (OAs) of the housing-audit study [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] deposited their replication package in the collection of the *American Journal of Political Science* on the Harvard Dataverse, under the persistent identifier [doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU) and a CC0 dedication, which places the files in the public domain. The [repositories module](repositories.qmd#sec-dataverse) reads the record itself: its files, its blinding of the community variables and its two versions. Here the task is only to get the data file.

**By hand.** The DOI opens the record. The file `HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.tab` is listed among the six files, and its *Access File* menu offers it as tab-separated text, the form into which Dataverse converts every tabular file, or in its *Original File Format*, the Stata file that the OAs deposited. Either will do; the Stata file keeps the labels of the variables.

**Through the API.** Every Dataverse installation answers requests from programs at fixed addresses, and the `dataverse` R package (version 0.3.16 on CRAN, released in November 2025 and developed on GitHub under IQSS, the Harvard institute that builds the Dataverse software) wraps those requests in functions. Two calls list the files of the record and read the data file straight into a data frame:

```{r}
#| eval: false
files <- dataverse::dataset_files("doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU", server = "dataverse.harvard.edu")

audit <- dataverse::get_dataframe_by_name(
  "HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.tab",
  dataset = "doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU",
  server = "dataverse.harvard.edu",
  original = TRUE,      # the Stata file that the OAs deposited, not the tab-separated copy
  .f = haven::read_dta  # the function that reads it
)
```

`audit` then holds `r format(nrow(audit_original), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(audit_original)` columns, one row per email. The same record answers without the package, because every file has a DOI of its own, and the access address of the API returns a file by that DOI. The snapshot of the record that the course keeps lists them:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dataverse
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The six files of the record doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU (version 1.1), as the native API of the Harvard Dataverse lists them. The size and the MD5 sum of the data file are those of the deposited Stata original. Queried on 27 October 2026 by `companion/_model-outputs/build_dataverse_files.R`."
dv_files |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(File = "label", DOI = "file_doi", Bytes = "bytes", MD5 = "md5")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::format_tt(j = "Bytes", digits = 0, num_fmt = "decimal", num_mark_big = ",") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = c("DOI", "MD5"), fontsize = 0.8)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
url <- paste0("https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/:persistentId",
              "?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU/TCBRDW&format=original")
utils::download.file(url, "HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.dta", mode = "wb")
tools::md5sum("HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.dta")
```

The last line should print `r dv_data$md5`, the MD5 sum that the record publishes for the data file. The copy that the course keeps in `data-raw/housing/` has the sum `r md5_archived`, so it is, byte for byte, the file that the OAs deposited. The first script of the pipeline of the case, `R/housing/01_audit_data.R`, reads that copy and writes the two CSV files of the course, `audit_original.csv` with the column names of the OAs and `housing_audit.csv` with readable names; the CC0 dedication is what allows the course to ship both in its workspace and to serve them in the browser lab.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Run the download above in any R session and compare the MD5 sum that it prints with the table. Then run `dataverse::get_dataset("doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU", server = "dataverse.harvard.edu")` and find the version number and the terms of use in what it returns. Which version would a citation of the record name today?
:::

### 3.2 The NCHS: the public-use files of the NSFG {#sec-nsfg}

The National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG) is run by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), part of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention of the United States. The original authors (OAs) of the cohabitation case [@KuoRaley2016DivergingPatternsUnion] drew on two of its surveys, 1995 (Cycle 5) and 2006–2010, and the course rebuilt their unions from the public-use female respondent files of those surveys and three later ones. The files are public. The CDC states that "Most of the information on the CDC and ATSDR websites is not subject to copyright, is in the public domain", no account is needed, and the use of the files is bound by the [data use restrictions](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data_access/restrictions.htm) of NCHS, which a user accepts by using them: "Use the data in this dataset for statistical reporting and analysis only", make no "intentional identification or disclosure of an individual", and "Not link this dataset with individually identifiable data from other NCHS or non-NCHS datasets." Files derived from them, such as the union file of the course, may therefore be shared, provided that they carry no identifier beyond the case number of the survey.

**What the files look like.** Each survey is a **fixed-width** text file (`.dat`): one line per respondent, every variable in the same columns of every line, with nothing between the values. The positions are given in **setup files**, programs for SAS, SPSS and (from 2002) Stata that read the data file, and the INPUT statement of the SAS setup file is the list that a reader in any language can use. Two of its lines for 2006–2010 give the start of the first cohabitation (`COHAB1`, columns 5636 to 5639), its status relative to the first marriage (`COHSTAT`, column 5640), its outcome and its duration:

```
   TIMESCOH  5634-5635      COHAB1  5636-5639        COHSTAT  5640
   COHOUT  5641             COH1DUR  5642-5644       HADSEX  5645
```

**The download.** The files are served from the server of NCHS at fixed addresses, so a few lines of base R fetch them, with `purrr::walk()` running the download once for each file. The 1995 file is about 142 MB and the 2006–2010 file about 77 MB:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# The 1995 file takes longer than the default limit of 60 seconds a download
options(timeout = 900)
nsfg_url <- "https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Datasets/NSFG"
nsfg_files <- c("1995FemRespData.dat", "2006_2010_FemResp.dat",
                "sas/1995FemRespSetup.sas", "sas/2006_2010_FemRespSetup.sas")
nsfg_dir <- "../nsfg_raw"  # a folder outside the workspace
dir.create(file.path(nsfg_dir, "sas"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
purrr::walk(nsfg_files, \(f) utils::download.file(file.path(nsfg_url, f), file.path(nsfg_dir, f), mode = "wb"))
```

The documentation is on the [NSFG pages](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/index.htm) of the CDC: a user guide and codebook for each survey, the specifications of the recoded variables, and the errata. One of the errata matters for the case. NCHS found that in 2006–2010 "respondents with 12 or fewer years of schooling (based on recode EDUCAT), a GED, and no higher degrees were incorrectly given a value on HIEDUC equal to EDUCAT rather than a value of 9", and published the correction in a [note](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nsfg/HIEDUC_correction_2006_2010.pdf) that the build of the course applies. A public file comes with its corrections, and a reanalysis that skips them works on a different file from the one that the agency now describes.

**Reading them.** Two CRAN packages read a fixed-width file through its SAS setup file, SAScii and asciiSetupReader. When the course pipeline was written, SAScii stopped on the encoding of the 2006–2010 setup file and placed some 1,100 variables of the 1995 file in the wrong columns, and asciiSetupReader stopped on all five files that the course reads. The course therefore takes the positions of the variables that it needs from the INPUT statement and reads them with `readr::read_fwf()`, which the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-cohabitation) shows step by step. The cohabitation three-day course downloads the two surveys in session 4 of [day 1](../tracks/cohabitation-three-days/day-1.qmd) and builds the unions from them on day 2.

### 3.3 The ESS Data Portal: rounds 1–4 {#sec-ess}

The European Social Survey is run by ESS ERIC, and its files are distributed through the ESS Data Portal at [ess.sikt.no](https://ess.sikt.no/en/), which Sikt, the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in Education and Research, runs for it. The original author (OA) of the immigration-and-trust case [@McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope] used rounds 1 to 4, fielded between 2002 and 2009, in sixteen countries. Searching and reading the documentation need no account, while downloading needs a free registration on the portal, which is best done in the week before the course.

**Which files.** The ESS publishes each round as an *integrated file* of every country whose data were ready when it was compiled, and releases a country that came later as a country file of its own. The Italian survey of round 2 was fielded in 2006 and is one of these, outside the integrated file of the round. Five files therefore make up the data of the case. Each edition of each file has a DOI of its own, which resolves to its page on the portal, and the course extract was built from these editions:

| File | Edition | DOI |
|---|---|---|
| ESS1 – integrated file | 6.7 | [10.21338/ess1e06_7](https://doi.org/10.21338/ess1e06_7) |
| ESS2 – integrated file (Italy not included) | 3.6 | [10.21338/ess2e03_6](https://doi.org/10.21338/ess2e03_6) |
| ESS2 – Italy country file from main questionnaire | – | [10.21338/ess2it](https://doi.org/10.21338/ess2it) |
| ESS3 – integrated file (Latvia and Romania not included) | 3.7 | [10.21338/ess3e03_7](https://doi.org/10.21338/ess3e03_7) |
| ESS4 – integrated file (Austria and Lithuania not included) | 4.6 | [10.21338/ess4e04_6](https://doi.org/10.21338/ess4e04_6) |

: The five ESS files of the immigration-and-trust case, with the editions from which the course extract was built. Source: the [codebook of the extract](../cases/trust/data/trust_ess_codebook.md).

**By hand.** Signed in, open each DOI, which leads to the page of the data file on the portal, and download the file in Stata format (`.dta`). Put the five files in one folder outside the workspace. The Stata files keep the labels of the answers and code the refusals, the "don't know" answers and the missing answers as missing values, which `haven::read_dta()` reads as `NA`.

**Through the API.** The portal has an API, which its [documentation](https://api.ess.sikt.no/docs) describes as "currently in beta" and as consisting of "a single endpoint, for downloading data files": a data file is requested by its DOI, with a user ID that the portal shows at [ess.sikt.no/en/api](https://ess.sikt.no/en/api) once you are signed in. The documentation states that the user ID "is _not_ for authentication – it is used to track usage statistics", and that "some larger data files are not available for download via the API". It identifies you all the same, so it belongs in the file `.Renviron` in your home folder, as a line `ESS_USER_ID=...`, and never in a script that you share. The five files then come down in one call of `purrr::iwalk()`, which runs the download once for each DOI and its name:

```{r}
#| eval: false
user_id <- Sys.getenv("ESS_USER_ID")
ess_dois <- c(ESS1e06_7 = "ess1e06_7", ESS2e03_6 = "ess2e03_6", ESS2IT = "ess2it",
              ESS3e03_7 = "ess3e03_7", ESS4e04_6 = "ess4e04_6")
ess_dir <- "../ess_raw"  # a folder outside the workspace
dir.create(ess_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
purrr::iwalk(ess_dois, \(doi, name) {
  # recodeMissingValues turns the codes of refusals and non-answers into missing values
  url <- paste0("https://api.ess.sikt.no/v1/data/dataFile/10.21338/", doi,
                "?userId=", user_id, "&fileFormat=dta&recodeMissingValues")
  utils::download.file(url, file.path(ess_dir, paste0(name, ".dta")), mode = "wb")
})
```

The R package that once did this, essurvey (version 1.0.8 on CRAN, of January 2022), was written for the download site that the ESS replaced with the portal on 30 May 2022. A report on its issue tracker warned in May 2022 that the package would stop working on that date, and rOpenSci, which hosts it, asked for a new maintainer in October 2022 because "a whole overhaul of the package is needed"; nothing has been released since. The course therefore uses the documented API with base downloads. The course team took its own copy of rounds 1–4 from a cumulative file of rounds 1–10 that it downloaded from the portal in March 2024, which carries the same editions, and the Italian country file beside it.

**The licence, and what an extract may do.** The terms are short and open. "European Social Survey data is licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0", and "European Social Survey documentation is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0". CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 allows anyone to share and adapt the data for non-commercial purposes, with attribution, provided that whatever is derived from them is shared under the same licence. A modified file must say so: "If a dataset is modified in any way, including translation changes, this should be indicated in the citation" in the form "'Adapted from ESS Round X, version number X'". And ESS ERIC asks for restraint in hosting copies: "ESS ERIC recommends that ESS datasets are not made available on external websites. ... If ESS datasets are stored externally, the version of the dataset should be clearly stated. ... Instead, please link to datasets on the ESS Data Portal." The course follows all three. Its extract, `trust_ess.csv`, selects respondents and variables, reverses the coding of several items, builds two vote controls and standardises household income, so its [codebook](../cases/trust/data/trust_ess_codebook.md) opens with "Adapted from ESS Rounds 1–4", lists the edition and DOI of each source file, releases the extract under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and sends anyone who wants the full files to the portal. The extract travels in the workspace under those terms, for non-commercial use only.

The file that Multi100 gave the five analysts of the case shows the other side of the same rule. It was built from the same ESS rounds by a SCORE reproduction and is public on the OSF ([osf.io/e48gd](https://osf.io/e48gd/)), but it states no licence, so the course does not ship it: the workspace downloads it when Task 3 needs it ([section 3.7](#sec-osf)). The immigration-and-trust three-day course downloads the five ESS files in session 4 of [day 1](../tracks/trust-three-days/day-1.qmd), and day 2 builds the extract from them as the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-trust) shows.

### 3.4 The GESIS archive: the Eurobarometer waves {#sec-gesis}

The outcomes of the EU-frames case are built from sixteen Eurobarometer waves between 2004 and 2013, the waves that included the question asking what the European Union means to the respondent personally, with its fourteen items. The files are distributed by **GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences**, the German social-science archive, which describes itself as "[the largest German infrastructure institute for the social sciences](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute)" and which runs the Eurobarometer Data Service for the European Commission. In the words of the service, "Eurobarometer data and documentation can be downloaded free of charge from the GESIS Data Catalog", and "the data are available to the scientific community for research and education" ([Eurobarometer Data Service](https://www.gesis.org/en/eurobarometer-data-service)). Every step below was checked in a browser on 8 September 2026, and the file downloaded from GESIS at the end was byte for byte identical to the one from which the course panel was built. The EU-frames three-day course downloads the sixteen files in session 4 of [day 1](../tracks/eu-frames-three-days/day-1.qmd), and the self-study track in [stage 10](../tracks/self-study/stage-10.qmd).

The sixteen studies are these. Every one is in the access category that GESIS labels "0 – Data and documents are released for everybody", which means a free account and nothing more; the file names are the ones that arrive in your download folder, and the two marked as zipped arrive as `.zip` archives that are unpacked by the course build script.

: The sixteen studies, with the versions current on 8 September 2026. GESIS re-releases files under new version numbers; the build script checks what you downloaded against this list.

The route is manual. Registration is a web form with a captcha, and every download asks for a purpose of use in your own name, so the steps below are clicked rather than scripted. A CRAN package, gesisdata (version 0.1.2, of July 2023), scripts the same clicks by driving a web browser through RSelenium, but it has not been updated since, and a report of a failed download, opened on its issue tracker in February 2025, has no answer, so the course does not rely on it.

**Before you start: two settings in the browser.** GESIS serves its pages in German by default and marks them as English, so Chrome quietly translates them into an English that differs slightly from the English version of the site, and the labels on your screen will not match the ones below. Turn translation off for the site (the translate icon in the address bar, then "Never translate this site") and click **English** in the page header. The sidebar then reads *Datasets / Questionnaires / Codebook* rather than *Datensätze / Fragebögen*.

![The catalogue as it first appears in a browser set to English: German, with the language switch at the top right.](../assets/gesis/00-german-default.jpg){.border}

**1. Register once, before the course.** Open [search.gesis.org](https://search.gesis.org/), click *Login* and then "You are not yet registered?". The form asks for your name, country, discipline, email and a password of at least eight characters with a capital letter, a number and a special character. There is one kind of account and no institutional check. The registration page states that "Registration at GESIS is free of charge, open to all". Registration is a web form with a captcha and cannot be scripted, which is why it should be done in the week before the course. One trap: the checkbox that says "I have read the GESIS Usage Regulations" links to the data-protection notice rather than the terms of use, which are at [gesis.org/en/institute/data-usage-terms](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute/data-usage-terms) and are summarised below.

![The registration form, upper half.](../assets/gesis/08-register-top.jpg){.border}

![The registration form, lower half, with the password rule and the two checkboxes.](../assets/gesis/09-register-bottom.jpg){.border}

**2. Find each study by its number.** Type the study number, `ZA4056`, into the search box and press Enter, and the search returns one hit. Do not search by wave name. "Eurobarometer 61.0" returns about nine hundred datasets with the 2023–2026 waves at the top and the one you want nowhere on the first page, and a `?q=` address pasted into the browser fills the box without running the search. The direct address `https://search.gesis.org/research_data/ZA4056` works too, and the table above links every study that way.

![Searching by wave name: nine hundred hits, the wanted study not among them.](../assets/gesis/01-search-wave-number.jpg){.border}

![Searching by study number: one hit.](../assets/gesis/02-search-za-number.jpg){.border}

**3. Read the study page.** It gives the title, the version, the DOI, the fieldwork dates and the countries, and, in the right-hand panel, three download links: *Datasets*, *Questionnaires* and *Codebook*. The questionnaires and the codebook download without an account; they are the documents that say which variable records which question in that wave, and the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-eu-frames) uses them.

![The study page of ZA4056, with the Downloads panel on the right.](../assets/gesis/03-study-page.jpg){.border}

**4. Download the Stata file.** Click *Datasets*. A dialog lists four files: an SPSS portable file, a syntax file defining missing values, the Stata file and the SPSS file. Take the Stata file only, the one ending in `.dta`. The course script reads that format with its labels, and the others are not needed. Above the list is a **Purpose of use** dropdown, in which you state a purpose in your own name. Choose "in the course of my studies" if you are a student, and "for further education and qualification" otherwise. The option "in a course as lecturer" is for the lecturer and not for participants. Signed out, the same click produces only a "Login required" box. Signed in, the file arrives under the name given in the table, with no further prompt.

![The download dialog, signed in, with the purpose-of-use dropdown and the four files.](../assets/gesis/04-download-datasets.jpg){.border}

![The same click when signed out.](../assets/gesis/07-login-required.jpg){.border}

**5. Put all sixteen in one folder** outside the workspace, and run the build script that the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-eu-frames) describes. It unpacks the two zipped studies, reads the sixteen files, checks each against the checksum of the file from which the course was built, and writes one respondent-level file into a folder that the workspace never commits.

**The terms you accepted.** The terms of use, valid since 4 February 2026, are the document to which every download dialog links, and four of their clauses shape how the course handles these files. Redistribution: "The provision of the database to third parties is not permitted", and third parties "include, but are not limited to, publishers, libraries, data archives, or research data repositories", so no respondent-level file goes into any repository, public or private. Identification: "The presentation or publication of individual cases, even if there is no direct reference to individuals, is not permitted", while "summary presentations of data, as is customary in scientific papers and lectures, are permitted", which is the line that separates the microdata from the aggregates distributed with this course. Citation: the DOI and the version number of each file must appear in anything published from them. The fourth clause bears on any course taught with AI assistants. It reads "The use of AI systems for processing the database provided to the user by GESIS is prohibited", with exceptions only on request. In practice that means the respondent file is never opened in a session that an AI assistant can read, never pasted into a chat, and never handed to an assistant that has access to the objects in your R session. The aggregates distributed with the course are not covered by this restriction. The terms also ask for deletion of the files at the end of the project, and put a contractual penalty of €10,000 on a breach of the redistribution and de-anonymisation clauses.

![The access categories, from the terms of use: the sixteen Eurobarometer studies are all in the first row.](../assets/gesis/06-access-categories.jpg){.border}

The terms permit the sharing of aggregates coarse enough that no respondent can be recovered, and those aggregates, released under their own licence, are all that this course shares from the Eurobarometer. The [data codebook](../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md) states that division in its licence section, CC BY 4.0 for the derived country-year panel, GESIS terms for everything beneath it. The rebuild for this course started from these sixteen files and averaged the respondents 'as interviewed', which is one of the choices offered at Level 2 of the specification menu. The [weights module](weighting.qmd) explains the alternative.

### 3.5 The macro indicators, at the World Bank {#sec-worldbank}

Two cases take their country-level series from the World Development Indicators of the World Bank, released under its open licence (CC BY 4.0). The EU-frames panel holds two of them:

- `unemp`: unemployment as a percentage of the total labour force, the national estimate, indicator `SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS`, which the Bank republishes from ILOSTAT;
- `growth`: annual GDP growth in percent, indicator `NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG`.

The immigration-and-trust case takes GDP per head and the modelled unemployment estimate of the ILO (`SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS`) from the same source, for the year before each round, because the OECD addresses that the paper gives no longer work; its pipeline queries the API of the Bank directly and keeps a dated snapshot of what it returned.

There are two ways to get a series. On the site, open [data.worldbank.org](https://data.worldbank.org/), search the indicator code, choose the countries and years and download a CSV. In R, the `WDI` package (version 2.8.0 on CRAN, released in August 2026) does the same in one call and returns a tidy country-year table:

```{r}
#| eval: false
macro <- WDI::WDI(
  country   = c("AT", "BE", "BG", "CY", "CZ", "DE", "DK", "EE", "ES", "FI", "FR", "GB",
                "GR", "HU", "IE", "IT", "LT", "LU", "LV", "MT", "NL", "PL", "PT", "RO",
                "SE", "SI", "SK"),
  indicator = c(unemp = "SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS", growth = "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"),
  start = 2004, end = 2013
)
```

The Bank publishes other estimates of the same quantity, among them the ILO modelled estimate, and Eurostat publishes its own series, built from the EU Labour Force Survey and fetched from the Eurostat database. The next section sets out the series that the EU-frames case uses besides the two above, and why two of them are not on the curve of the claim.

The third macro variable of the EU-frames panel, `bailout`, is not downloaded at all. It is coded from the record of EU and IMF financial assistance programmes, country by country and year by year, and the codebook lists the programmes and years used. Many contextual variables enter a panel in this way, through a documented rule applied by hand, with the source of each fact stated.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Run the `WDI` call above in your workspace and compare its `unemp` column with the one in `EUframes_cy.csv` for one country. They should agree to the decimal for most country-years and differ for a few, because the Bank revises series after the fact. Write down which years differ and by how much. Any macro series can change between downloads in this way, which is why the codebook records the download date.
:::

### 3.6 The published series {#sec-series}

The specification menu of the EU-frames case offers more than one published series for each of the two economic measures, and the decision sits at Level 2, among the decisions about measurement, because the series measure one construct, the national unemployment rate or the growth of output, in slightly different ways. For unemployment there are five: the national estimate of the World Bank above (`wb_nat`), which is the series of the course panel and of the reanalyst C6HJR, and four series cut from the Eurostat tables that the other reanalysts merged. Those are the rate in the labour force aged 15–74 from the table `une_rt_a_h` (`es_1574_act`, the series of 018OL), the unemployed as a share of the whole population aged 20–64 from the same table (`es_2064_pop`, KQXUE), the rate in the labour force aged 25–64 from the Labour Force Survey table `lfsa_urgan` (`es_2564_lfs`, the annual counterpart of the quarterly series of PRL47), and the rate in the labour force aged 15–74 from the short table `tipsun20` (`es_1574_tips`, KEVF1). For growth there are two, the World Bank series and the national accounts of Eurostat in the table `nama_10_gdp` (`es_growth`). All seven are held for the 270 country-years in `cases/eu-frames/data/macro/predictor_measures.csv`, so that the workspace can merge them without a connection, and the Eurostat tables are kept in the source repository as they were retrieved.

The four unemployment series that cover all 270 country-years differ in age band and denominator, and the population-based series of KQXUE is a different quantity from a labour-force rate, but within countries they move together. Once the mean of each country and of each year is removed, they correlate with one another at between `r cor_range[1]` and `r cor_range[2]`, so all four stay on the curve, where the choice among them carries `r measure_share` of the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlations.

The other two series left the curve, because choosing either of them changes who is in the analysis as well as how the economy is measured. The table `tipsun20` has rows for `r coverage$cells[coverage$measure == "es_1574_tips"]` of the 270 country-years, in `r coverage$countries[coverage$measure == "es_1574_tips"]` countries, with none for the United Kingdom and, before 2009, rows for only `r paste(tips_pre, collapse = " and ")`. Choosing it therefore halves the panel and moves the question towards the crisis years: swapped into the `r tips$n_pairs` unemployment specifications of the curve, it leaves `r tips_below` of them below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r curve_below` of the unemployment specifications on the curve itself, and it changes the class of `r tips_changes` of the pairs. It is a decision about the sample presented as one about the measure, which is why the [decision map](../cases/eu-frames/map.qmd) rewrites the population in the estimand statement when the series is chosen. The Eurostat growth series has no row for the United Kingdom, `r coverage$cells[coverage$measure == "es_growth"]` country-years in `r coverage$countries[coverage$measure == "es_growth"]` countries, which costs one country for the same reason, although within the countries that it covers it moves with the World Bank series and leaves the class of every one of its `r es_growth$n_pairs` pairs unchanged. Coverage of this kind is worth checking before any series is merged, since a merge that silently drops rows changes the population of the question without changing a line of the model.

### 3.7 The OSF: the files of SCORE and Multi100 {#sec-osf}

The Open Science Framework holds the dossiers that SCORE kept on each of the four papers and the components in which the Multi100 analysts left their materials, and the [repositories module](repositories.qmd#sec-score-dossiers) reads those dossiers as records. Three of the cases take a file from them. A public file on the OSF needs no account: every file has a short address of five characters, such as `b6p3j`, and `https://osf.io/download/` followed by that address returns the file itself. The `osfr` package (version 0.2.9 on CRAN, of September 2022; its development continues on GitHub under rOpenSci) reaches the same files through the API of the OSF and lists the contents of a project or a component. The three files:

- **The cohabitation case: the person-month file of SCORE**, `Estimation Data - Kuo (JWzJ).csv` at [osf.io/b6p3j](https://osf.io/b6p3j/), which SCORE built for its replication of the paper and which Multi100 gave each of the five analysts. It is public, the report of the replication states that "All materials on this OSF project may be shared publicly", and the course ships it in the workspace as `score_person_months.csv`.
- **The immigration-and-trust case: the file of the analysts**, `McLaren_SRD_final_data.csv`, a file of the SCORE reproduction [osf.io/e48gd](https://osf.io/e48gd/), which Multi100 gave the analysts. It holds respondent-level ESS data and states no licence, so the workspace fetches it from `https://osf.io/download/yehpm/` when Task 3 needs it, into a folder that git ignores, and checks its MD5 sum.
- **The EU-frames case: the course panel**, `EUframes_cy.csv` in the main folder of [osf.io/6zqct](https://osf.io/6zqct/), the fork of the Multi100 record of analyst C6HJR that the facilitator maintains. The workspace script `R/get_data.R` fetches it with osfr as an exercise, and falls back to the committed copy when the network or the OSF is down.

The two routes, for the file of the cohabitation case:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# osfr: the file by its address, then the download
score_file <- osfr::osf_retrieve_file("b6p3j")
osfr::osf_download(score_file, path = "data_private")

# base R: the download address of the same file
utils::download.file("https://osf.io/download/b6p3j/", "score_person_months.csv", mode = "wb")
tools::md5sum("score_person_months.csv")
```

The MD5 sum of the copy that the analysts received, recorded in the [codebook](../cases/cohabitation/data/score_person_months_codebook.md) of the file, is `2b656d3814d273f4a93e29bc4f0139ef`, and a download by either route gives that sum. A checksum is computed from the bytes of a file, so a program that rewrites the ends of the lines of a text file changes it without changing a single value; git on Windows does that to CSV files unless it is told otherwise, which is why a value-by-value comparison, as in the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-trust-check), is the safer check of a text file that has passed through a repository. `osfr::osf_ls_files(osfr::osf_retrieve_node("jkzdq"))` lists the other files of the same component: the data dictionary, the script of the replication, its printed results and the paper.

The OSF itself is changing. From 19 February 2027 every OSF project becomes read-only, so these files will still download at the same addresses indefinitely, but no project will receive new ones. The maintained copy of the EU-frames panel from then on is the [`replication-lab`](https://github.com/CodeMoreh/replication-lab) repository on GitHub, and the [repositories module](repositories.qmd#sec-osf) sets out what the change means for depositing your own work.

## 4. Citing data {#sec-citing}

A dataset is cited like a publication, with the producer, the title, the version or wave, the distributor and the persistent identifier, and most archives print the citation that they want on the study page. The four cases show the range:

- **The Harvard Dataverse** prints a citation for every dataset, with its version and a **UNF**, a checksum that Dataverse computes from the values in the data rather than from the bytes of the file, so that the same data saved in another format give the same UNF. The citation of the housing-audit package names the version that it used.
- **The ESS** gives a citation for each data file, with its edition and DOI, and asks that a modified file be cited as "Adapted from ESS Round X, version number X"; the [codebook of the trust extract](../cases/trust/data/trust_ess_codebook.md) carries both for its five source files.
- **NCHS** gives no DOI to the NSFG files, so a citation names the agency, the survey, the cycle and the file, with the date of download; the [codebook of the union file](../cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_unions_codebook.md) does that.
- **GESIS** asks for the study number, the DOI and the version of each wave, which the table of section 3.4 gives for the sixteen of the EU-frames case.
- **The World Bank** asks for the indicator and the date of access.

Two further habits help a reader who wants to repeat your analysis. Record the date on which you downloaded a series, because the World Bank and Eurostat revise past years without renaming the file, and a reader who repeats your download a year later will get slightly different numbers. And keep the version identifier of a survey file, because the ESS, SHARE, the NSFG and the Eurobarometer all release corrected editions of the same round, as the correction of the education variable of the NSFG in [section 3.2](#sec-nsfg) shows.

## Sources {#sec-sources}

The access rules of the map were read from the pages of the archives themselves on 8 September 2026: the [types of data access](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/help/access-policy/types-of-data-access/) page of the UK Data Service, which names the Open, Safeguarded and Controlled tiers, the End User Licence, the Special Licence and SecureLab; the [microdata pages of Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/microdata), which describe research-entity recognition, the proposal step, scientific-use and secure-use files; the [SHARE data access page](https://share-eric.eu/data/data-access); the [IPUMS International](https://international.ipums.org/) front page, from which the coverage figures are quoted; and the [ESS Data Portal](https://ess.sikt.no/en/). The GESIS pages (the terms of use with their access categories, the Eurobarometer Data Service page, the registration form and the study pages) were read in a browser on the same day, as [section 3.4](#sec-gesis) describes. The ICPSR pages could not be read by the tools used to prepare this module, so the description of ICPSR in the table above rests on the long-standing arrangements of the archive and should be checked against its current pages before you rely on it.

The routes of the four cases were checked on 27 October 2026. The Dataverse record was queried through its native API and through the `dataverse` package, and the data file downloaded both ways matched the MD5 sum that the record publishes. The NSFG files were downloaded for the course from the server of NCHS on 26 October 2026, with the terms quoted from the pages of the CDC and of NCHS on that day, and their addresses were checked again on 27 October. The ESS licence was read from the [disclaimer page](https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/contact/disclaimer) of the ESS on 26 October 2026, and the API of the portal from its [documentation](https://api.ess.sikt.no/docs) on 27 October; the API was not called, because it needs the user ID of a registered user. The OSF files were downloaded with osfr and with base R on 27 October 2026 and matched their recorded MD5 sums. The versions and dates of the R packages (`dataverse`, `WDI`, `osfr`, `essurvey`, `gesisdata`, SAScii, asciiSetupReader) were read from their pages on CRAN on 27 October 2026, and the state of essurvey and gesisdata from their issue trackers on GitHub. The provenance of the data of each case is recorded in its codebooks: the [housing-audit file](../cases/housing/data/housing_audit_codebook.md), the [union file](../cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_unions_codebook.md), the [ESS extract](../cases/trust/data/trust_ess_codebook.md) and the [EU-frames panel](../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md).
